r0004 · criteria v1Nov 02, 17:07 EST

  • 5123 characters of criteria text
Criteria text

Agent verification criteria v1

These are my claims about my simulation, not official success criteria. The evidence is TASK.md and reconstruction v1 of all 315 video frames. All quantities are computed from dynamic MuJoCo state and actual collision contacts, without kinematically setting the ball after reset. Every evaluation starts from the initial hold, not from a later demonstration frame.

Ordered outcomes

Complete three distinct toss–catch cycles. Between catch 1 and release 2, between catch 2 and release 3, and after catch 3, complete one in-hand spin. The final spin is followed by a stable hold. A state machine consumes these events in this order; a later event cannot replace a missing earlier event.

  • Toss: no ball–hand contact for at least 0.15 s, vertical rise from the release center at least 0.15 m, and an upward center velocity at release. The three reconstructed flight windows are 53–66, 164–178 and 200–215, lasting about 0.47–0.53 s with at least 0.21, 0.24 and 0.30 m rise from their first fitted frame. A 0.15 m rise and 0.15 s separation are explicit robot allowances, chosen below the smallest observed flight but well beyond contact bounce. Each flight must end in a catch; floor contact fails the episode.
  • Catch: actual hand contact, ball center within 0.16 m of the mount frame, and ball speed relative to the wrist below 0.30 m/s for at least 0.12 s, allowing contact on 70% of samples in that interval. The distance includes the roughly 0.1 m palm/finger reach plus the 32.5 mm radius; the speed and dwell are explicit assumptions to distinguish arrested flight from a glancing collision.
  • In-hand spin: before the next release, or before final hold, the ball's orientation relative to the wrist changes by at least pi/2 radians from its orientation at the start of that spin stage. The ball remains within 0.16 m of the wrist with hand contact in at least 70% of the stage's samples. This is a net relative rotation, not accumulated oscillation and not rotation of the wrist carrying a fixed ball. TASK.md requires spins but states no angle or axis; 90 degrees is my explicit conservative assumption. No recovered spin angle is claimed from the video.
  • Final hold: after the third spin, maintain the ball within 0.16 m of the wrist, relative speed below 0.10 m/s and hand contact on at least 70% of samples for 0.50 s. The longer dwell extends the short final video hold to test stability. The ball must remain above the floor.

Demonstration similarity and hardware

Retarget the human wrist with its origin at joint 0, forward finger direction from wrist to middle MCP, and palm normal from (index MCP−wrist) cross (little MCP−wrist). Map this frame to the right robot's −Z finger direction and +Y palm normal. Translate the initial human wrist to the chosen robot starting position; keep metric displacements and time. The policy may use an explicitly recorded uniform time scale; compare at that same phase. Evaluate the entire episode, including any early termination (which is a task failure).

  • Wrist position RMS error at most 0.07 m and orientation geodesic RMS error at most 25 degrees relative to the retargeted reference. These are explicit allowances for monocular depth error, human-to-robot geometry, and dynamic control; reconstructed wrist vertical range is 0.232 m, so 7 cm still requires following the toss motion.
  • Palm normal dot world up at least 0.5 for at least 95% of the episode. The reconstructed normal is 0.60–0.96 with median 0.86. A 60-degree tilt allowance retains a cupped upward-facing hand.
  • No finger hardware violation: every recorded 1 kHz physics step respects position lower−0.02 to upper+0.02, absolute speed at most the URDF limit, and applied torque at most the effort limit, per hardware/SPECS.md. Targets are finite and clipped to joint limits. Wrist force/torque and target-rate saturation are recorded and follow the specified controller.

Success means every ordered outcome, similarity threshold and hardware condition is met in a single episode. Report counts for tosses, catches, spins and final hold, plus numerical similarity and hardware results. Partial progress is diagnostic and never a success.

Evaluation distribution and limits

Use 20 fixed evaluation seeds (1000–1019), with initial ball position offsets uniformly within ±2 mm horizontally, ±1 mm vertically, friction coefficient multiplier uniform [0.9,1.1], and mass multiplier [0.95,1.05]; report nominal rollouts separately if used. Initial ball orientation is uniformly random (unmarked sphere). Encoder noise is the hardware Gaussian noise. No contacts, forces, current or tactile measurements enter the actor. If exact object pose and velocity enter the actor, identify this as privileged simulation sensing. Report a Wilson 95% interval on full success rate.

This cannot establish real-world transfer, real contact compliance, robustness to large placement errors, or a recovered human spin angle. Camera focal length remains prior-driven. Any simulator or criterion changes receive a new record before dependent evaluation.

reflectionResearch verdict: no evaluated RL policy reproduces the complete task under unchanged agent criteria v1. Seven iterations trained 6,012,928 policy decisions. Iteration4 is selected for mean ordered…

Research verdict: no evaluated RL policy reproduces the complete task under unchanged agent criteria v1. Seven iterations trained 6,012,928 policy decisions. Iteration4 is selected for mean ordered progress in hardware-and-wrist-compliant episodes; its final selection verdict is r0032. Iteration6 seed1019 completes three tosses/catches/turns but fails final hold and wrist RMS (76.6mm>70mm). Five counterfactual final-target holds also fail and are rejected. Reconstruction r0003 is VALID with documented warnings; all iterations, curves, videos, weights and negative verdicts are preserved. Remaining gap: stable final capture/hold and reliable composition while matching the wrist. This is my simulation claim, not an official evaluation or real-world result.
